995.title: Eisai
995.hook: brings Rinzai Zen and tea seeds back from China
995.howItsDone: In Rinzai Zen temples, tea is served as part of the daily schedule and at ceremonies, and the tea ceremony that later developed in Japan kept close ties to Zen.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shinran's family, and a teacher who called himself neither monk nor layman.

The young shogun, in his capital at Kamakura, has a terrible morning after a night of drinking. Someone is sent for, and a Buddhist monk arrives carrying two things: a bowl of tea, and a little book he has written about tea and health. The shogun drinks, and, according to a chronicle of the time, feels better, and is pleased with the book. It is a small scene. But the monk carrying the bowl had brought home from China a lineage of Zen practice and, tradition says, the seeds of tea plants too. His name was Eisai.
screen: `A SHOGUN'S BAD MORNING.` → `A BOWL OF TEA AND A LITTLE BOOK.` → `EISAI.`

segments.voice: First, the journey. Eisai was trained as a monk in the Tendai school on Mount Hiei, the same mountain where Honen studied. He traveled to China looking for the living roots of the teaching, and there he received the Linji line of Chan. In Japanese, Linji is pronounced Rinzai. So the true person of no rank, from a few days ago, comes home with him. Tradition remembers Eisai as the one who brought Rinzai Zen to Japan. Second, the seeds. Tradition also says he carried tea seeds back from China and planted them, and that tea gardens grew from them. Whether every story about those seeds is exact, his love of tea is in his own words. Third, the book. He wrote a short work on drinking tea for health, the Kissa Yojoki. It opens by calling tea a wonderful medicine for nourishing life. For him, tea was medicine first, a way to keep the body well. It was practical, not decorative. Fourth, the pair. Eisai also wrote in defense of Zen, arguing that its practice could serve and protect the country. So he came home with two gifts that would, over time, grow into each other: a way of sitting, and a way of drinking a cup.
screen: `FROM MOUNT HIEI TO CHINA.` · `LINJI BECOMES RINZAI.` · `TEA SEEDS, AND A BOOK ON TEA.` · `TWO GIFTS: SITTING AND A CUP.`

996.title: The old cook
996.hook: the young Dogen meets an old monastery cook drying mushrooms in the sun who won't let anyone else do it
996.howItsDone: In Soto Zen monasteries, Dogen's Instructions for the Cook guides the kitchen, and the tenzo prepares meals as a form of practice, with care for each ingredient and the people who will eat.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Eisai, who came home from China with a Zen lineage and, tradition says, tea seeds.

Mushrooms, spread out to dry on a stone walkway at a Chinese monastery. The midday sun is fierce, and the stone is hot enough to feel through sandals. Out on it, bent over them, is the monastery's cook. He is old, his eyebrows white, no hat, a bamboo staff in his hand, sweat running down his face. A young Japanese monk, visiting to study, stops and stares. Why is this old man doing this, now, himself? The young monk was Dogen, and he wrote the scene down years later. Today, tenzo.
screen: `A FIERCE MIDDAY SUN.` → `AN OLD COOK DRYING MUSHROOMS.` → `YOUNG DOGEN STOPS AND STARES.`

segments.voice: First, the job. The cook in a Zen monastery, the tenzo, was not a kitchen hand. It was a senior post, held by an experienced monk, because feeding the community was treated as practice of the highest seriousness. Dogen wrote a whole work about it, Instructions for the Cook, and this meeting is at its heart. Second, the question. Dogen asked the old man why he didn't have a helper or a worker do it. The cook answered, in Dogen's telling: others are not me. Your line comes from that. Not someone else. Third, the follow-up. Dogen pressed: fine, but why now, in the worst of the heat? The cook said: if not now, when? Dogen had no reply. He wrote that only then did he begin to understand what the cook's work really was. Fourth, what it means. The cook isn't refusing help out of pride. His practice is his own, and it happens in this hour, with these mushrooms. Handing it off, or putting it off until a better time, would be handing off his own life. For Dogen, who had come all the way to China looking for the teaching in scriptures and great halls, it was a surprise to find it on a hot walkway, in an old man's sweat. In this telling, the kitchen, the sink, even the inbox, are not interruptions to practice. They are the practice, and no one else can do yours.

997.title: Just sitting
997.hook: Dogen: just sit; sitting itself is awakening
997.carry: like a car passing outside the window
997.howItsDone: In Soto Zen temples and sitting groups, people sit zazen facing a wall or the room, upright on a cushion, without counting the breath or working on a koan, and some groups recite Dogen's instructions on sitting together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tenzo: the old cook drying mushrooms in the hot sun, who wouldn't hand the job to anyone. Your line: not someone else.

A young monk comes home to Japan from China, and people want to know what he brought back. Scrolls? Statues? Relics? In a talk recorded years later, Dogen says he came home empty-handed. All he brought back, he said, was that the eyes are horizontal and the nose is vertical. It sounds like a joke, and maybe it is. But it points at what he taught for the rest of his life: nothing extra, no treasure hidden somewhere else. Just this face, this body, this cushion.

The word is shikantaza, a Japanese term usually rendered just sitting, or nothing but sitting. In a short text on how to sit, Dogen keeps it plain. Find a quiet room. Sit on a thick cushion, upright, leaning neither left nor right, forward nor back. Breathe quietly. Then let go of the whole wheel of thinking: don't judge thoughts good or bad, don't chase them, don't push them away. Here's the turn. For Dogen, this sitting is not a ladder you climb to reach awakening somewhere above it. Practice and awakening are not two things. You don't sit to get enlightened later, the way you'd save money for a car. The sitting itself is awakening, showing up right now in a body on a cushion. So nothing gets added: no counting, no picture, no question to solve, no goal held out in front. Dogen also passes on an old exchange. A monk asks a teacher what he thinks about, sitting so still. The teacher says he thinks of not-thinking. How do you think of not-thinking? Non-thinking. Thoughts arrive and leave, and nobody grabs them. Soto Zen, which looks back to Dogen, keeps this sitting at its center. It's the difference between waiting for a bus and simply sitting at the bus stop.
screen: `SHIKANTAZA: NOTHING BUT SITTING.` · `UPRIGHT, QUIET, LETTING THOUGHTS GO.` · `NOT A LADDER TO AWAKENING.` · `PRACTICE AND AWAKENING, NOT TWO.` · then, large: `THINK OF NOT-THINKING.`

segments.voice: Sit upright the way Dogen describes, not stiff, not slumped, hands resting, and let the breath breathe itself without counting it. When a thought arrives, a plan, a worry, a song, let it come and go like a car passing outside the window; if you notice you've followed one down the street, that noticing is fine too. Come back to just this body, sitting here, with nothing to get and nothing to fix.
Shikantaza. Just sitting, nothing added, which Dogen taught is awakening itself rather than a road toward it. Today's word.

998.title: To study the self
998.hook: Dogen: to study the way is to study the self, to study the self is to forget the self (Genjokoan)
998.howItsDone: Zen students study the Genjokoan with teachers and in study groups, and some temples chant or read it aloud; teachers often point students back to it during sitting retreats.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shikantaza: just sitting, with nothing added. Your line was like a car passing outside the window.

Someone sits in a small boat, looking at the shore. The trees seem to slide past. The dock drifts away. For a moment it really looks as if the land is moving. Then they glance down at the water against the hull, and it's obvious: the boat is what moves. Dogen uses this picture in a short essay called Genjokoan. When we look at the world with a confused idea of ourselves, he says, we get the movement backward.
screen: `THE SHORE SEEMS TO MOVE.` → `LOOK AT THE BOAT.` → `GENJOKOAN.`

segments.voice: Here is the heart of it, in plain words. Dogen writes, roughly: to study the Buddha way is to study the self. To study the self is to forget the self. To forget the self is to be confirmed by all things. One step at a time. First, the path isn't a subject out there, like geography. What you're studying is the one doing the studying: how your attention moves, what you grab, what you flinch from. Second, the surprise. Look closely enough at the self and it stops being the solid thing at the center of everything. Forgetting here isn't amnesia or self-hatred. It's closer to being so absorbed in kneading bread or fixing a bike chain that the little narrator who comments on everything goes quiet. Third, once the narrator steps back, the world isn't scenery sliding past you. The dough, the chain, the sound of the street show up fully, and you're part of what's happening instead of watching from a booth. That's the boat again: a self that thinks it's standing still while everything else moves has the picture upside down. Dogen adds that even the traces of awakening are left behind, not held onto. Readers have worked on these lines for a long time, and they don't all read them the same way. But the sequence is clear on the page: study, forget, be confirmed.
screen: `STUDY THE WAY: STUDY THE SELF.` · `STUDY THE SELF: FORGET THE SELF.` · `FORGETTING: THE NARRATOR GOES QUIET.` · `FORGET THE SELF: ALL THINGS CONFIRM.` · then, large: `STUDY. FORGET. BE CONFIRMED.`

segments.voice: For a few minutes, let breathing be the one task you forget yourself in: feel the breath arrive at the nose, fill the chest, and leave. Each time the narrator starts up, how am I doing, what's next, don't fight it; just hand the attention back to the breath, the way you'd hand a tool back to someone mid-job. See whether, for a breath or two, there's only breathing.
Genjokoan. Dogen's essay teaching that to study the way is to study the self, and to study the self is to forget it. Today's word.
Your line: forget the self. The little narrator can rest. That's day nine hundred ninety-eight.

999.title: Being-time
999.hook: Dogen: time isn't something you pass through; you are time
999.howItsDone: Zen students read Dogen's Uji with a teacher, slowly and often more than once, and bring its questions into zazen and into daily work in the temple.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Genjokoan: to study the self is to forget the self, and the boat that only seemed to stand still. Your line: forget the self.

Where did this morning go? We talk about time like a river, with us on the bank watching hours float away. We spend it, save it, waste it, kill it, run out of it. Time is outside us, and we're the ones it happens to. Dogen wrote an essay that turns this around. Readers of Dogen explain that he took an ordinary Japanese word meaning something like sometimes, or at a certain time, and read its two characters side by side: being, and time.
screen: `TIME AS A RIVER.` → `WE WATCH IT GO.` → `DOGEN TURNS IT AROUND.`

segments.voice: The essay is called Uji, being-time. Its claim, put plainly: time is not a container things sit inside. Things are time, and time is things. The pine tree is time, Dogen says in effect, and the bamboo is time. Mountains are time, oceans are time, and so is the person sitting here. Your life isn't moving through the hours; this breath is the hour. He gives a picture. You cross a river and climb a mountain. Afterward, the river and the mountain seem behind you, gone, and you're up here in the present. That's only one way of seeing it, Dogen says. The crossing and the climbing were being-time, fully, when they happened, and they don't simply vanish into a back room. In the Genjokoan, in the same collection, he writes about firewood and ash. We say firewood becomes ash. But firewood has its own place as firewood, with a before and an after, and yet cut off from them. Ash has its own place too. Each moment stands complete. Readers explain this in different ways. Some hear impermanence turned inside out: nothing lasts, so each moment is entire. Others hear a point for sitting: you can't wait for awakening later, because later isn't a separate place. Either way, the question changes. Not where did the time go, but what is this time being, right now?
screen: `UJI: BEING-TIME.` · `PINE IS TIME, BAMBOO IS TIME.` · `THE RIVER AND THE MOUNTAIN.` · `FIREWOOD HAS ITS PLACE, ASH HAS ITS PLACE.` · then, large: `THIS TIME IS YOUR LIFE.`

segments.voice: Sit, feel the weight in the seat and the air on your skin, and notice when the mind leans forward toward later, or back toward earlier. Then come to this breath, not one on the way to something, but the whole of what your life is doing right now. If it helps, say silently with the in-breath, this is time, and with the out-breath, this is my life.
Being-time. Dogen's word, uji, for time and being as one thing: the pine, the mountain and you, not inside time but as time. Today's word.

1000.title: Nichiren
1000.hook: the monk who taught chanting the Lotus Sutra's title, Namu Myoho Renge Kyo
1000.howItsDone: Nichiren Buddhists chant Namu Myoho Renge Kyo, called the daimoku, often morning and evening before a scroll called the Gohonzon, and recite passages from the Lotus Sutra; groups meet in homes and temples to chant together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, being-time: the pine is time, the mountain is time, and so are you. Your line: you are time. And today is day one thousand.

In homes and community centers, people kneel or sit before a scroll and chant one phrase, steadily, again and again, a rolling rhythm that can fill a room: Namu Myoho Renge Kyo. No long instructions to memorize, no complicated posture. Just a phrase, a voice and a scroll. That chant goes back to a Japanese monk who said the title of one sutra held the whole of the Buddha's teaching.
screen: `ONE PHRASE, CHANTED.` → `NAMU MYOHO RENGE KYO.` → `A MONK WHO PICKED A TITLE.`

segments.voice: Nichiren was a monk in Japan who studied widely and came to one conviction: the Lotus Sutra was the Buddha's highest teaching, and the way into it was its title. Tradition says he first chanted the phrase aloud at his home temple, facing the sunrise. Open the phrase. Namu means something like devotion, or I take refuge in. Myoho is the wonderful law, or mystic law, the truth the sutra teaches. Renge is the lotus, which grows out of mud and blooms clean. Kyo is sutra, a teaching. Myoho Renge Kyo is the sutra's title; namu is the devotion placed in front of it. Together: devotion to the Lotus Sutra of the wonderful law. Why a title? In Nichiren's teaching, the title isn't a label on the outside of a book. It holds the whole sutra, the way a seed holds a tree. So chanting it meets the entire teaching with your own voice, not only your eyes or your intellect, which opens the practice to anyone, not just scholar monks. Nichiren was outspoken. He wrote that Japan's troubles came from turning away from the Lotus, he argued hard with the schools of his day, and tradition remembers that he was sent into exile for it. Today his followers belong to several groups, including Nichiren Shu, Nichiren Shoshu and Soka Gakkai, which differ on how to read his teaching and who carries it forward. What they share is the chant. For Nichiren Buddhists, saying the title isn't a warm-up for practice. It is the practice.
screen: `A MONK AND ONE SUTRA.` · `NAMU, MYOHO, RENGE, KYO.` · `THE TITLE HOLDS THE WHOLE.` · `SEVERAL GROUPS, ONE CHANT.` · then, large: `THE CHANT IS THE PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, chant the title three times at an easy, steady pace, the way Nichiren Buddhists do: Namu Myoho Renge Kyo, Namu Myoho Renge Kyo, Namu Myoho Renge Kyo. If saying it isn't right for you, simply hear it in your head. Then let it go quiet, and feel what the sound leaves behind in the chest, the throat, the room.
Nichiren. The Japanese monk who taught that the title of the Lotus Sutra, Myoho Renge Kyo, holds the whole teaching, and that chanting Namu Myoho Renge Kyo is the practice. Today's word.
Your line: the title of the Lotus. A whole teaching, held in a name. A thousand days on the path, and still walking.

1001.title: Ikkyu
1001.hook: the wild Zen poet-monk who mocked pomp
1001.howItsDone: Ikkyu is remembered in Japan through his poems, his calligraphy and folk stories, and Zen students and teachers read his verse as a reminder not to confuse the robes and ranks of practice with practice itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nichiren, and a whole sutra held in its title: Namu Myoho Renge Kyo. Your line: the title of the Lotus.

A Zen monk walks through town in shabby robes, and people say he drinks in taverns and writes poems that would make an abbot blush. He calls himself Crazy Cloud. Stories say that when his teacher offered him the certificate that proves a student's awakening, he wouldn't keep it. Another has him at New Year, while everyone celebrates, carrying a skull on a stick through the streets as a reminder. Not all these tales can be checked. But they all point the same way.
screen: `SHABBY ROBES, TAVERN POEMS.` → `NO CERTIFICATE.` → `A SKULL AT NEW YEAR.`

segments.voice: Ikkyu was a Japanese Rinzai Zen monk and poet, remembered more through his poems, gathered in what's known in English as the Crazy Cloud Anthology, than through any sermon. First, what he aimed at. His poems jab at monks who wear fine robes, collect titles, sell certificates of awakening and run temples like businesses. For him, all that ceremony could become a costume over an empty room. Zen was supposed to strip things down to the plain truth, and here it was dressing up. Second, how he aimed: not with a treatise, but with laughter, scandal and verse. His poems talk openly about wine, love and the body, things a respectable monk was supposed to keep quiet about. Readers argue about how literally to take them. Some hear a monk refusing to pretend he's purer than he is. Others hear a teacher using shock the way a Zen master uses a shout, to knock a student loose. Third, the twist. Tradition says that late in life Ikkyu was asked to lead Daitokuji, the kind of temple he'd mocked, and he took up the work of rebuilding it. The wild monk didn't drop out of the tradition. He loved it enough to laugh at it. And that closes the week: Eisai's tea, the old cook in the sun, Dogen's just sitting, forgetting the self and being-time, Nichiren's chant, and now Ikkyu's laugh. Each is its own path, but side by side they share a small thread: meet what's here, without the extras.
screen: `A POET-MONK: CRAZY CLOUD.` · `FINE ROBES, EMPTY ROOMS.` · `LAUGHTER, SCANDAL AND VERSE.` · `HE LOVED IT ENOUGH TO LAUGH.` · then, large: `DROP THE EXTRAS.`

segments.voice: Sit easily and bring to mind one small way you dress yourself up: a title you like to mention, an opinion you defend a bit too loudly, the version of yourself you post. Look at it kindly, the way Ikkyu might from a tavern doorway, and let a smile come if it wants to. You don't have to throw it away; just see the costume as a costume, and rest in whatever is under it.
Ikkyu. The Japanese Zen poet-monk who called himself Crazy Cloud and used laughter and verse to puncture pomp. Today's word.
Your line: the wild monk. He laughed at his own tradition because he loved it. Until tomorrow.
